title: 2017 AMC 12B Problem 13
statement: In the figure below, \(3\) of the \(6\) disks are to be painted blue, \(2\) are to be painted red, and \(1\) is to be painted green. Two paintings that can be obtained from one another by a rotation or a reflection of the entire figure are considered the same. How many different paintings are possible?

solutions.text:
Before accounting for symmetry, there are \(\dfrac{6!}{3!2!}=60\) paintings. The two nonidentity rotations partition the disks into two \(3\)-cycles, so neither can fix a painting having color counts \(3,2,1.\)

Each of the \(3\) reflections fixes \(2\) disks and swaps the other \(4\) in \(2\) pairs. For a painting to be fixed, the lone green disk and one of the \(3\) blue disks must occupy the two fixed positions, in \(2\) orders. Of the two swapped pairs, either one can be the red pair, giving \(2\cdot2=4\) fixed paintings per reflection. Burnside’s Lemma therefore gives \(\dfrac{60+3(4)}{6}=12\) distinct paintings.

Thus, the correct answer is D.
hints: Count the labeled colorings first, then apply Burnside’s Lemma to the \(6\) symmetries of the triangle
A nonidentity rotation fixes none; under a reflection, the odd green and blue counts must use the two fixed disks
